newsitem.title: RUSSIA: SOCCER-BAN SETS RUSSIAN RESORT UP FOR SOCCER FEST.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-BAN SETS RUSSIAN RESORT UP FOR SOCCER FEST.

text.p: The Black Sea town of Sochi, once the communist elite's favourite resort, is in for a mass spring migration of Russian soccer when the 1997 season opens next week after officials on Tuesday upheld a ban on icy northern pitches.

Nikita Simonyan, first vice president of the Football Union, said appeals had been rejected from some of the eight premier league clubs ordered to play their first two home games on neutral grounds after failing to install undersoil heating.
The decision, part of the league's bid to stamp out icebound pitches, has set up two double bills on the opening weekend.
Sochi's own Zhemchuzhina host champions Spartak Moscow on March 16, followed by penalised Rotor Volgograd playing their "home" tie against Chernomorets Novorossiisk.
The next day two more offenders, both newly promoted, provide a second double-header. Dynamo-Gazovik Tyumen take on Rostselmash Rostov and Fakel Voronezh play Zenit St. Petersburg.
Also in mild southern Russia, the third premiership newcomers, Shinnik Yaroslavl from the northern Volga, will play their first "home" game against Torpedo Moscow at Krasnodar.
Rotor, who finished third last season, were particularly upset by the ruling, emphasising that their relatively southerly pitch is already in perfectly good condition.
Volgograd official Alexander Pavlov told Reuters: "The whole city has waited all through a long winter to see Rotor play and this decision is not in the interests of soccer."
The ruling favours the five big Moscow clubs who dominate the championship, since they play most home games at just two stadiums -- Dynamo and Lokomotiv -- which already have heating.
Valery Frolov, president of Shinnik Yaroslavl, told Reuters the installation of heating under his pitch would cost around $200,000, about a 10th of the club's entire annual budget.
But failure to do so by September will mean the deduction of six points, which could mean relegation, he added.

The big Russian clubs are pressing the league to switch to a west European autumn-to-spring calendar to improve their chances in European competitions. But the smaller provincial teams say that is impractical given Russia's long, harsh winter.
